questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents a magnified sector of a young microsporangium wall in a transverse section of an anther, showing four wall layers (labelled P, Q, R, and S) surrounding the central sporogenous tissue (T).

Which labelled layer nourishes the developing pollen grains and generally possesses cells with dense cytoplasm and more than one nucleus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic shows a cross-sectional sector of a young microsporangium with four concentric wall layers ordered from outside to inside as P, Q, R, and S, enclosing the central mass of cells labelled T.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a standard transverse section of an angiosperm microsporangium, the layers are arranged sequentially from the outermost protective covering toward the central sporogenous tissue.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A typical microsporangium is surrounded by four wall layers: epidermis (outermost), endothecium, middle layers, and tapetum (innermost). The outer three layers perform protection and help in anther dehiscence, while the innermost layer nourishes the developing pollen grains.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Label P is the outermost layer, representing the epidermis.
2. Label Q is the second layer beneath the epidermis, representing the endothecium.
3. Label R represents the middle layers.
4. Label S is the innermost wall layer directly bordering the central sporogenous tissue (T); this is the tapetum, whose cells have dense cytoplasm and are generally multinucleate (or binucleate) to nourish developing pollen grains.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying the radial sequence from outside to inside confirms that S is the tapetum. Therefore, layer S (Tapetum) nourishes the developing pollen grains.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Parts of a typical anatropous ovule

questiontext.text:
Study the diagrammatic view of a typical anatropous ovule shown below, with four regions labelled W, X, Y, and Z.

Which of the following correctly identifies W, X, Y, and Z?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic depicts an inverted (anatropous) angiosperm ovule with four labelled structures: W (the supporting stalk), X (the junction between the stalk and the ovule body), Y (the small opening left by the integuments at the tip), and Z (the basal region opposite the opening).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In an anatropous ovule, the body of the ovule is inverted so that the micropylar opening lies close to the stalk, while the basal region lies at the opposite pole.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By definition: the ovule attaches to the placenta via a stalk called the funicle; the junction between the ovule body and funicle is the hilum; the small opening not covered by integuments is the micropyle; and the basal part opposite the micropylar end is the chalaza.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. W points to the stalk of the ovule, which is the funicle.
2. X points to the region where the body of the ovule fuses with the funicle, which is the hilum.
3. Y points to the small apical opening between the integuments, which is the micropyle.
4. Z points to the basal end opposite the micropyle, which is the chalaza.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Cross-checking each anatomical landmark confirms the sequence: W: Funicle, X: Hilum, Y: Micropyle, Z: Chalaza.

answer.text: W: Hilum, X: Funicle, Y: Chalaza, Z: Micropyle
W: Funicle, X: Hilum, Y: Micropyle, Z: Chalaza
W: Funicle, X: Micropyle, Y: Hilum, Z: Nucellus
W: Chalaza, X: Hilum, Y: Micropyle, Z: Funicle

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Mature embryo sac structure and ploidy

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows a mature angiosperm embryo sac (7-celled, 8-nucleate). Observe the labelled structures K, L, M, N, E, and F.

Which labelled structure guides the entry of the pollen tube into the synergid, and what is the ploidy of each nucleus in the pair labelled M prior to triple fusion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a mature 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac oriented with the chalazal end at the top and the micropylar end at the bottom. Three cells (K) are at the chalazal end, a large central cell (L) holds two central nuclei (M), and the micropylar egg apparatus contains an egg cell (E) and two synergids (N) with special cellular thickenings (F) at their micropylar tips.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The embryo sac (female gametophyte) develops via monosporic development from a single haploid functional megaspore through three rounds of free-nuclear mitosis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Mitotic divisions of a haploid megaspore produce 8 haploid (\(n\)) nuclei. At the micropylar tip of the synergids, special cellular thickenings called the filiform apparatus guide the pollen tube into the synergid.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Structure F represents the filiform apparatus at the micropylar tip of the synergids (N), which guides the entry of the pollen tube.
2. Pair M represents the two polar nuclei situated in the large central cell (L).
3. Because all nuclei in the embryo sac arise by mitosis from the single haploid (\(n\)) functional megaspore, each polar nucleus in M is haploid (\(n\)) prior to triple fusion.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
During triple fusion, these two haploid (\(n\)) polar nuclei fuse with one haploid (\(n\)) male gamete to form a triploid (\(3n\)) primary endosperm nucleus, confirming that each polar nucleus is haploid (\(n\)). Thus, structure F (Filiform apparatus) guides the pollen tube, and each nucleus in M is haploid (\(n\)).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Longitudinal section of a grass embryo

questiontext.text:
The schematic below illustrates the longitudinal section (L.S.) of a monocotyledonous embryo of grass, with structures labelled P, Q, R, and S.

Which combination correctly identifies P, Q, and S along with their respective structural roles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram presents a longitudinal section of a grass (monocot) embryo showing a large lateral structure (P), a hollow foliar sheath (Q) surrounding an upper meristematic apex (R), and a lower undifferentiated sheath (S) enclosing the radicle and root cap.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In monocotyledonous embryos of the grass family, the embryonal axis is oriented vertically with the epicotyl (shoot end) toward the top and the hypocotyl/radicle (root end) toward the bottom, while the single cotyledon lies laterally.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In grass embryos: (1) the single lateral cotyledon is termed the scutellum; (2) the epicotyl has a shoot apex and leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure called the coleoptile; (3) at the lower end of the embryonal axis, the radicle and root cap are enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called the coleorrhiza.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. P is the prominent lateral structure attached to one side of the embryonal axis, identifying it as the scutellum (single lateral cotyledon).
2. Q is the hollow foliar sheath enclosing the shoot apex (R), identifying it as the coleoptile.
3. S is the undifferentiated sheath enclosing the radicle and root cap at the lower end, identifying it as the coleorrhiza.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Confirming the anatomical positions (lateral cotyledon, upper shoot sheath, lower root sheath) establishes that P is the scutellum, Q is the coleoptile, and S is the coleorrhiza.

answer.text: P: Coleoptile (food-storing cotyledon), Q: Scutellum (sheath around plumule), S: Root cap (protective tip)
P: Scutellum (lateral cotyledon), Q: Coleorrhiza (sheath around shoot apex), S: Coleoptile (sheath around radicle)
P: Epiblast (reduced cotyledon), Q: Coleoptile (sheath around radicle), S: Coleorrhiza (sheath around shoot apex)
P: Scutellum (single lateral cotyledon), Q: Coleoptile (hollow foliar sheath enclosing shoot apex), S: Coleorrhiza (undifferentiated sheath enclosing radicle and root cap)
